newsitem.title: SPAIN: Basque leaders urge ETA rebels to declare truce.
newsitem.headline: Basque leaders urge ETA rebels to declare truce.

text.p: The government of Spain's Basque region called on ETA guerrillas on Saturday to follow the example of the Irish Republican Army and declare a truce, saying the time had come to "put a stop to the killing."

The appeal for an end to ETA's campaign of terror was issued one week after separatist rebels sparked national outrage by killing town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco. Bells rang out in unison from churches and town halls across Spain in continuing protest against the murder.

Declaring that "the decision is clearly in ETA's hands," Basque leaders issued their plea for the rebels to "silence their weapons" shortly after the IRA announced a new truce to take effect in Northern Ireland on Sunday.
"The public outcry of the past week points precisely in that direction," Basque Interior Minister Juan Maria Atutxa said.

Millions of Spaniards, incensed by the murder of an ordinary, low-ranking functionary, have taken to the streets to vent their anger. Pope John Paul and other world leaders have also condemned the killing.
Atutxa said ETA was now faced with "an historic moment and a chance to give a future of peace and hope to this people."
"If these intolerant, violent people come to the realization it's time to put a stop to the killing and their crimes...all democrats will agree to it," he said.

Atutxa urged ETA's political arm, Herri Batasuna, to support the call for a truce just as the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein had backed such a move by the guerrillas in Northern Ireland. A spokesman for Herri Batasuna declined comment.

The Basque government called for a truce of "indefinite" duration, but a leading Basque nationalist politician, Inaki Anasagasti, said ETA would have to disavow violence for at least one year to prove its desire for peace was genuine.

The last ETA truce lasted for only one week in 1996. The rebels ended it after rejecting the government's demand that they must renounce violence before any negotiations could take place. The guerrillas then mounted a series of bomb attacks on tourist resorts.
Many Spaniards stood in silence as bells rang for five minutes beginning at 4 p.m. on Saturday in a show of solidarity for Blanco's family and of condemnation for his killers.

Blanco's killing exactly one week earlier mobililised public opposition in a way never seen in ETA's 29-year history of armed struggle. The group has killed nearly 800 people in its fight for an independent homeland encompassing parts of northern Spain and southern France.
Memorial masses and anti-ETA rallies were held in several cities and scores of people in a town in southern Spain launched a hunger strike described as a protest against "all kinds of terrorism."

Former leaders of Colombia's M-19 leftist guerrilla group, which mounted daring attacks in the 1980s before giving up the fight, called on ETA to "listen to the Basque people's shout for peace, unity and freedom."

The outcry against ETA extended to cyberspace. An Internet site accused of sympathising with the guerrillas was "mailbombed" out of existence on Friday by an avalanche of electronic mail sent by anti-ETA computer users.
